expansion:
Optokinetic drum testing is the keyed answer for a 2-year-old because it does not require the child to name letters or point: the examiner watches for reflex following (nystagmus-like) eye and head movements as a rotating striped drum passes in front of the child, which works in a preverbal toddler who cannot cooperate with a chart-reading task. This specific method is not printed in the lecture material (not taken from the course material); the lecture's acuity-testing content is built entirely around the standard adult/cooperative-patient tools — the Snellen chart, the Landolt-C chart and the tumbling-E chart on slide 113 — and the deck explicitly contains no content on paediatric or preverbal acuity testing methods, with the transcription noting zero mentions of children, infants or illiterate-patient charts anywhere in the file (L1,2, slide 113 area).

Snellen's chart, option A, requires the patient to read printed letters aloud and report line by line, which demands literacy and verbal cooperation that a 2-year-old does not have; the lecture presents it as the standard literate-adult acuity chart (L1,2, slide 113), not as a paediatric tool.

Landolt's chart, option B, substitutes a broken ring ("C") whose gap direction the patient must indicate instead of naming a letter, which removes the literacy requirement but still needs the child to understand and perform a matching or pointing task; the lecture lists it alongside Snellen's chart as one of the three standard acuity charts without describing any adaptation for toddlers who cannot yet follow such instructions (L1,2, slide 113).

Electroretinogram, option D, is an electrophysiological test of retinal function (photoreceptor and inner retinal responses) rather than a measure of visual acuity; it can detect retinal disease even in an uncooperative or preverbal patient, but it does not quantify how well the child sees, so it is not a visual acuity test at all (not taken from the course material).
objective: Identify optokinetic drum testing as an acuity assessment method usable in a preverbal 2-year-old, as distinct from chart-based tests that need cooperation or verbal response
